paragraphs: Why can classifying a time series by its nearest known example work so well? This paper develops an explanation based on a latent source model: many observed sequences may arise from a relatively small collection of underlying patterns. Having many examples of those patterns could make simple comparisons effective.

The model leads to a weighted voting rule, in which training examples contribute to a classification decision, and nearest-neighbor classification approximates that rule. The authors establish finite-sample performance guarantees for both methods under their model. These guarantees account for the amount of a sequence observed and the complexity of its underlying sources, connecting early prediction to the assumed structure of the data.

In synthetic experiments, weighted voting reaches the same classification error as nearest neighbors using shorter observations. Applied to Twitter news topics, it detects trends before Twitter 79% of the time, averaging an advantage of 1 hour and 26 minutes. The reported true-positive and false-positive rates are 95% and 4%, respectively. These results demonstrate early forecasting in the studied setting.
neurips-2013-a-latent-source-model-for-n.tldr: A model with relatively few underlying time-series patterns explains simple classifiers and supports early trend forecasting.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is useful for large optimization problems, but randomness in its gradient estimates can slow its progress as training continues. This paper introduces stochastic variance reduced gradient, or SVRG, to address that obstacle directly. Its central idea is to reduce the variability in stochastic updates so that randomness interferes less with convergence.

For objectives that are smooth and strongly convex, the authors prove that SVRG achieves the same fast convergence rate as stochastic dual coordinate ascent and Stochastic Average Gradient. These conditions define the scope of the stated guarantee. The paper also presents its analysis as simpler and more intuitive, making the reason for the acceleration easier to understand.

A practical distinction is that SVRG does not require storing gradients as the compared methods do. That reduces a storage burden that can complicate more elaborate learning problems. The authors identify some structured prediction problems and neural network learning as settings where this makes the method easier to apply. The broader contribution is a variance-reduction approach combining a conditional convergence guarantee with practical flexibility.
neurips-2013-accelerating-stochastic-gra.tldr: SVRG reduces stochastic-gradient variance, achieving fast convergence for smooth, strongly convex objectives without requiring stored gradients.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling updates variables using their relationships with other variables. Those dependencies often force standard updates to run sequentially, restricting parallel computation even when many relationships are weak. Hogwild sampling relaxes this coordination: processors update variables in parallel and communicate globally only periodically. The paper asks when this strategy remains well behaved.

The authors study Gaussian distributions and build a framework giving convergence conditions and error bounds. Connections to numerical linear algebra help explain the behavior and support relatively simple proofs. Focusing on this distribution family provides a concrete setting in which the consequences of reduced coordination can be analyzed.

A central result concerns Gaussian precision matrices that are generalized diagonally dominant. Under that sufficient condition, any Hogwild update schedule and any assignment of variables to processors produce a stable sampling process with the correct sample mean. The conclusion specifically establishes stability and mean accuracy; it does not equate these properties with exact recovery of the entire distribution. The result clarifies one substantial setting where aggressive parallelism has theoretical support.
neurips-2013-analyzing-hogwild-parallel-.tldr: For Gaussian models satisfying a stated precision-matrix condition, Hogwild Gibbs sampling remains stable and preserves the correct mean.

paragraphs: Estimating many regression parameters is only part of a statistical analysis; researchers also need to know how uncertain those estimates are. In high-dimensional problems, nonlinear estimation procedures make the distribution of an estimate difficult to characterize exactly. This complicates the construction of confidence intervals and significance tests.

The paper proposes an efficient method for a broad class of regression problems by constructing a de-biased version of regularized M-estimators. Regularization supports estimation, while the correction creates a basis for uncertainty calculations. The resulting algorithm produces confidence intervals and p-values, connecting fitted parameter values to classical tools for assessing statistical evidence.

The authors establish nearly optimal interval sizes and nearly optimal power for testing whether a parameter is zero. These claims concern both precision of uncertainty statements and ability to detect nonzero parameters. Their construction improves on recent work by avoiding a special structural assumption on the design matrix. They also report simple proofs and test the method on a diabetes prediction problem, illustrating its use in an applied regression setting.
neurips-2013-confidence-intervals-and-hy.tldr: De-biasing regularized regression estimates enables efficient confidence intervals and hypothesis tests with nearly optimal statistical properties.

paragraphs: Hidden-layer prediction models learn intermediate features between inputs and outputs. This can give them expressive power, but it also makes training difficult: the hidden variables and the model parameters must be inferred together. Their interaction creates a highly nonconvex optimization problem, where local training methods can struggle to find good solutions.

This paper develops a convex relaxation of hidden-layer conditional models. A relaxation reformulates the optimization problem so that global training becomes possible within the new formulation. The approach extends convex modeling to accommodate two nested nonlinear transformations with an adaptive latent layer between them. That intermediate layer remains a substantive part of the model.

The resulting methods can learn two-layer models whose behavior cannot be represented by a single-layer model using the same features. The authors also report improved training quality relative to local heuristics. Together, these findings connect expressive hidden representations with a more globally tractable training formulation. The global-training claim applies to the convex relaxation, which is the paper's proposed route around the original optimization difficulty.
neurips-2013-convex-two-layer-modeling-3.tldr: A convex relaxation allows global training of expressive two-layer prediction models with an adaptive hidden layer.

paragraphs: Music recommenders often learn from listening or other usage patterns. That creates a cold-start problem for songs with no usage history: the system lacks the behavioral evidence it normally uses. This paper investigates whether a song's audio can supply the representation needed to recommend it.

The approach uses a latent factor recommendation model, where songs have learned representations that support recommendations. When usage data cannot provide those factors, a model predicts them from audio. The authors compare a traditional bag-of-words audio representation with deep convolutional neural networks. Both approaches address the same task of translating sound into factors relevant to listener preferences.

Evaluation on the Million Song Dataset includes quantitative and qualitative assessments. Predicted factors yield sensible recommendations, despite the substantial gap between an audio signal and the musical characteristics that influence preference. Deep convolutional networks significantly outperform the traditional approach in the reported comparison. The findings support audio-based factor prediction as a way to extend a usage-based recommendation framework to songs lacking the usual behavioral information.
neurips-2013-deep-content-based-music-re.tldr: Predicting recommendation factors from audio helps address song cold starts, with deep convolutional networks outperforming a traditional audio representation.

paragraphs: When observations are counts, choosing what to measure can be as important as analyzing the resulting data. This paper studies measurement design for a vector Poisson model. A linear projection acts on a nonnegative vector of underlying rates, and the observations are counts associated with those projected rates.

The authors choose the measurement matrix by maximizing mutual information, a measure of how much the observations reveal about a target. They consider two targets: the full rate vector and an associated latent class label. These objectives distinguish measurements intended to preserve information about a signal from measurements intended to help identify its category.

The technical contribution is new analytic expressions for the gradients of both information objectives with respect to the measurement matrix. These expressions make it possible to guide measurement design using the objective's sensitivity to matrix changes. The paper also connects the count setting to Gaussian measurement models. Examples cover document topic modeling through word counts and chemical classification through hyperspectral photon counts, showing how the formulation applies to different kinds of counting data.
neurips-2013-designed-measurements-for-v.tldr: Information-based gradients guide the design of Poisson count measurements for learning either an underlying signal or its class.

paragraphs: EDML was introduced as a method for learning Bayesian-network parameters, but its original explanation required approximate inference on a separate meta-network. That derivation helped uncover the algorithm and its properties, while also bringing considerable conceptual complexity. This paper offers a simpler way to understand the same approach.

The authors recast EDML as a general method for continuous optimization. From this perspective, some results that previously required substantial proofs become immediate. The reformulation also makes it easier to design related learning algorithms for other graphical models, turning an explanation of one method into a framework for extending it.

Using that framework, the paper derives an EDML algorithm for parameter learning in Markov networks. Empirical results show that, on complete data, it can sometimes produce better estimates several times faster than conjugate gradient and L-BFGS. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is an observed possibility in the evaluated setting. The contribution combines conceptual simplification with a concrete extension from directed to undirected graphical models.
neurips-2013-edml-for-learning-parameter.tldr: Viewing EDML as continuous optimization simplifies its theory and enables a Markov-network learning algorithm with promising empirical results.

paragraphs: Learning how discrete variables depend on one another can require different information from learning each variable's individual distribution. Copula methods separate these two modeling tasks. When individual distributions are ancillary to the goal, extended rank likelihood goes further by using observable order information and bypassing explicit models for those distributions.

The computational difficulty appears during Bayesian inference with Gaussian copulas. Rank information imposes constraints on the space being sampled, and the number of constraints grows quadratically with the number of observations. Standard Gibbs sampling moves slowly through this constrained space, making the dependence-learning procedure expensive to carry out effectively.

This paper introduces an efficient sampling algorithm based on constrained Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo. The authors describe it as straightforward to implement and able to avoid a quadratic cost in sample size. Its contribution is computational: it makes inference for rank-based dependence models more manageable. The motivation applies when marginal information is unnecessary for the learning objective, including the dimensionality-reduction and copula-parameter tasks identified in the abstract.
neurips-2013-flexible-sampling-of-discre.tldr: Constrained Hamiltonian sampling makes rank-based discrete dependence inference more efficient without modeling individual variable distributions.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with multiple related components. Labeling every component of every training example can demand substantial annotation effort. This paper develops active learning algorithms that request labels for only selected parts of an output, aiming to learn useful models with much less supervision.

The selection rule uses the entropy of local marginal distributions. These distributions describe uncertainty about individual output variables, and their entropy serves as a proxy for where additional labels may be informative. By making queries at this local level, the method can direct annotation effort toward particular variables rather than requiring a complete output annotation each time.

The authors demonstrate the approach on predicting three-dimensional layouts from single images. In that application, good models can be learned from labels for relatively few variables. They report matching the performance obtained with the full training set while labeling approximately 10% of the random variables. This empirical result supports selective partial annotation as an effective strategy for the studied task, linking local uncertainty estimates to a substantial reduction in labeling.
neurips-2013-latent-structured-active-le.tldr: Selecting uncertain parts of structured outputs for labeling matches full-training performance with about 10% of variable labels in a layout-prediction study.

paragraphs: A useful recognition representation should tolerate changes in an object's appearance while retaining information that distinguishes its identity. This paper proposes a model for learning such representations across identity-preserving transformations. It extends beyond the translation and scaling changes commonly handled by convolution and includes other convolutional networks as special cases.

The model's connections can be learned from videos showing objects transform, or from image groups organized by object identity. The authors examine both invariance and discriminability through increasingly complex tests. They first confirm theoretical predictions empirically for two-dimensional affine transformations, then study non-affine changes relevant to face verification.

The model performs well when faces rotate in depth or illumination direction changes. It also tolerates changes in background clutter, an empirical finding that motivates further evaluation in unconstrained settings. Tests on Labeled Faces in the Wild, PubFig, and a newly collected dataset show strong performance. These results support the usefulness of learning from identity-linked image groups, while keeping the broad modeling capability distinct from the particular transformations tested.
neurips-2013-learning-invariant-represen.tldr: Learning from identity-linked images produces representations that handle several appearance changes and perform strongly on face verification tasks.

paragraphs: Distributed learning workers need access to shared model values, but waiting for fresh values can consume time that could otherwise be spent computing. This paper proposes a parameter server organized around Stale Synchronous Parallel computation, or SSP. The server provides a shared interface for reading and writing model parameters and variables.

SSP allows workers to read older values from local caches instead of repeatedly waiting for central storage. It controls this flexibility by placing a maximum age on the values a worker may use. That bound makes staleness an explicit part of the computation model and supplies the mechanism through which the authors establish correctness.

The paper provides a correctness proof under SSP and evaluates the system on several machine-learning problems. The reported experiments show faster algorithm convergence than fully synchronous and asynchronous alternatives, alongside more time spent computing instead of waiting. The findings illustrate how bounded delays can improve distributed learning: workers gain freedom to continue useful computation while the system retains a defined constraint on how outdated their information can become.
neurips-2013-more-effective-distributed-.tldr: A parameter server with bounded stale reads reduces worker waiting while supporting correctness and faster convergence in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A neural circuit can receive several kinds of sensory input while communicating through spikes. This paper studies how a single circuit can encode multiple stimuli together and how those inputs can subsequently be recovered. Its model combines a bank of multisensory receptive fields with a population of biophysical spike generators.

The authors demonstrate that stimuli with different dimensions can be faithfully combined in a shared spike representation. They derive tractable algorithms that recover each stimulus from the common spike pool. This makes the encoding question concrete: the representation must preserve enough information to separate the different inputs during decoding.

The paper also connects decoding to identifying the sensory processing performed by a neuron. It establishes a duality between identifying a single multisensory neuron and recovering inputs encoded by a population. A proved limit is that identification reveals only the circuit's projection onto the input stimuli, constraining what those observations can establish about the circuit. An example using natural audio and video illustrates the framework, and the authors discuss decoding and identification performance.
neurips-2013-multisensory-encoding-decod.tldr: A spiking circuit model supports joint multisensory encoding and decoding while establishing a limit on identifying the underlying circuit.

paragraphs: Networks change as relationships appear, disappear, or shift among entities. This paper seeks a summary of both their shared structure and their evolution. Its guiding idea is that changes among groups of nodes help explain changes in the observed network, with individual nodes able to belong to multiple groups.

The proposed model combines three components. A distance-dependent Indian Buffet Process represents group births and deaths. A Factorial Hidden Markov model describes how individual nodes' memberships evolve. An explicit connectivity model links those changing memberships to the network's relationships. Together, these components distinguish changes in which groups exist from changes in who belongs to them and how they connect.

The authors demonstrate identification of evolving latent groups across several types of network data. Experiments also report higher predictive performance for forecasting future networks and predicting missing links. These findings suggest that representing group dynamics can help with both interpretation and prediction in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a unified account of evolving group structure and the relationships it helps explain.
neurips-2013-nonparametric-multi-group-m.tldr: A dynamic multi-group model tracks group creation, disappearance, membership changes, and connectivity to explain and predict evolving networks.

paragraphs: Distributed learning algorithms must decide how much to coordinate concurrent work. Strict coordination constrains which operations can happen together, while very loose coordination permits more overlap. This paper investigates an intermediate approach based on optimistic concurrency control, bringing explicit conflict handling into the design of distributed learning algorithms.

The approach begins with the working assumption that conflicts are unlikely. Computation proceeds optimistically, and a resolution protocol is invoked when a conflict actually arises. This makes conflict management responsive to events instead of relying entirely on advance restrictions. The authors argue that this organization is particularly appropriate for large-scale machine learning, especially unsupervised learning.

The paper develops the approach in clustering, feature learning, and online facility location. These applications provide distinct settings in which to examine how optimistic execution and conflict resolution can be incorporated into learning procedures. The methods are evaluated through large-scale experiments in a computing cluster. The contribution is the intermediate concurrency strategy and its demonstration across these problems, with conflict resolution serving as an integral part of the algorithms.
neurips-2013-optimistic-concurrency-cont.tldr: Optimistic concurrency control lets distributed learning proceed under an assumption of rare conflicts and resolves conflicts when they arise.

paragraphs: Learning bounds can use more than the average loss observed in data. This paper introduces an inequality that also benefits from low empirical variance, meaning relatively little variation in the observed losses. It combines a PAC-Bayesian bounding technique with an Empirical Bernstein bound to make that information useful.

The authors compare the resulting PAC-Bayes-Empirical-Bernstein inequality with the PAC-Bayes-kl inequality. When empirical variance is substantially smaller than empirical loss, the new bound is significantly tighter. Otherwise, the bounds are comparable. The advantage is therefore tied to a property of the observed losses, giving a specific condition under which the new construction is especially valuable.

The paper identifies regression as a particularly useful application and presents the result as an application of PAC-Bayesian techniques to self-bounding functions. Empirical comparisons use a synthetic example and several UCI datasets. The central significance is that observed variability can sharpen a learning guarantee: two situations with similar average loss need not warrant equally loose bounds when their empirical variances differ.
neurips-2013-pac-bayes-empirical-bernste.tldr: A variance-sensitive PAC-Bayesian bound is substantially tighter than PAC-Bayes-kl when empirical variance is much smaller than empirical loss.

paragraphs: A knowledge graph records facts as relationships between pairs of entities. Given an incomplete graph, the task is to predict additional true relationships. This paper introduces a neural tensor network to model these facts more expressively, addressing weak entity interactions and simple linear projections in earlier approaches.

The model lets entity representations and relations interact multiplicatively. This provides a richer way to represent how a pair of entities fits a particular relationship. The authors also represent an entity by averaging vectors for the words in its name. Shared words then provide an additional source of similarity through which entities can share statistical strength.

Evaluation asks the model to classify unseen relationships using a partial knowledge base. It outperforms previous models in the reported experiments, reaching 86.2% accuracy on WordNet and 90.0% on FreeBase. These findings support combining richer relational interactions with information from entity names. The demonstrated reasoning task is knowledge-base completion: using observed relationships and learned representations to assess additional candidate relationships.
neurips-2013-reasoning-with-neural-tenso.tldr: Neural tensor networks combine multiplicative relational interactions with entity-name representations to improve knowledge-base completion.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares probability histograms through a transportation problem: how their mass can be moved between locations. Although this formulation has appealing properties, computing it requires solving a linear program. The paper identifies that computation as prohibitively expensive once histogram dimensions extend beyond a few hundred.

The proposed approach introduces an entropy regularization term into the classical transportation problem. This smooths the optimization and gives it a maximum-entropy interpretation. The resulting formulation can be computed using Sinkhorn's matrix scaling algorithm, providing a different computational route to transport-based comparisons.

The authors present a new family of transportation distances and report computation several orders of magnitude faster than transportation solvers. They also report better performance than competing distances on the MNIST benchmark. These findings concern both the cost of computing comparisons and their usefulness in the evaluated task. The paper's central contribution is to connect an entropy-modified transport objective with an efficient matrix-scaling procedure, making transport-based histogram comparison substantially more practical in the reported setting.
neurips-2013-sinkhorn-distances-lightspe.tldr: Entropy regularization enables Sinkhorn matrix scaling to compute transport-based histogram distances far faster, with improved reported MNIST performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation of a high-dimensional inverse covariance matrix when its structure is sparse. The proposed procedure, ALICE, is semiparametric and applies to the elliptical family of distributions. Its design addresses both statistical estimation and the computational work required to fit a large matrix.

A central feature is calibration of regularization separately when estimating each matrix column. This adapts the regularization across the estimation problem instead of leaving its treatment disconnected from the columns being fitted. For computation, the authors develop a dual inexact iterative projection algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM.

The theory establishes the parametric convergence rate for both parameter estimation and model selection. ALICE is also asymptotically tuning free, and the authors report improved finite-sample performance. The asymptotic statement concerns its behavior as sample size grows, while the finite-sample result addresses practical estimation with limited data. Simulations support the theory, and a real-data example illustrates the estimator's effectiveness. Together, calibration and efficient optimization form the method's main contribution.
neurips-2013-sparse-inverse-covariance-e.tldr: ALICE calibrates columnwise regularization for sparse inverse covariance estimation, combining convergence guarantees with efficient optimization.

paragraphs: Understanding how a neuron responds to a high-dimensional stimulus requires capturing which stimulus patterns matter and how they combine. The generalized quadratic model represents this through linear receptive fields, a low-rank quadratic combination, an invertible response transformation, and exponential-family noise. It can also incorporate dependencies on earlier spikes.

For canonical-form models, the authors derive approximate maximum-likelihood estimators by spectrally decomposing the first two response-weighted moments. The derivation uses an expected log-likelihood quantity and extends moment-based approaches such as spike-triggered covariance. For Gaussian noise, they obtain closed-form estimators across a large class of non-Gaussian stimulus distributions.

The reported estimators are highly accurate while requiring much less computation than full maximum likelihood. This makes the approach useful for fitting multidimensional stimulus sensitivity without paying the full optimization cost. Applications include analog membrane-potential recordings from V1 and retinal spike-train recordings. These examples show the framework being used with both continuous neural measurements and discrete spiking responses, connecting its statistical construction to different forms of neural data.
neurips-2013-spectral-methods-for-neural.tldr: Spectral estimators fit generalized quadratic neural-response models accurately at much lower computational cost than full maximum likelihood.

paragraphs: Interactions between time series can be nonlinear, and each observation may itself be a vector, graph, or string. This paper develops a statistical framework for analyzing such interactions when observations come from stationary time series. That setting retains temporal structure while allowing a broad range of data types.

The framework uses a kernel cross-spectral density operator built from positive definite kernels. Kernels allow the analysis to work across arbitrary input domains, while the operator provides a basis for studying coupling between sequences. The authors use it to construct both an independence test and a similarity measure for comparing different forms of coupling.

The independence test is evaluated against an HSIC test using independent-and-identically-distributed assumptions. The reported comparison shows improved detection errors and supports the approach's suitability for complex dynamical systems. The authors also apply it to electrophysiological neural time series. The contribution is a unified way to test and compare temporal interactions in complex data, with stationarity defining the stated setting for the analysis.
neurips-2013-statistical-analysis-of-cou.tldr: Kernel cross-spectral operators support dependence testing and coupling comparisons for stationary time series of complex observations.

paragraphs: A graphon is a limiting object associated with a convergent sequence of graphs and can generate random graphs. It provides a nonparametric way to describe network structure beyond a fixed parametric model. This paper addresses the estimation problem that comes with that flexibility: recovering the underlying graphon from observed graphs.

The authors propose a computationally efficient algorithm based on approximating the graphon with stochastic block models. The block-model representation supplies a structured approximation to an otherwise more general object. This connects a tractable modeling approach to the broader goal of estimating a nonparametric source of random graphs.

The main theoretical result is consistency: the graphon can be estimated so that the estimation error tends to zero as graph size tends to infinity. The observations in the stated problem are a set of graphs generated from the underlying graphon. The result establishes a large-graph recovery guarantee for the approximation strategy. Its significance is that computationally manageable block models can serve as a route toward recovering this more flexible underlying network description.
neurips-2013-stochastic-blockmodel-appro.tldr: An efficient stochastic-blockmodel approximation consistently estimates a graphon as the size of generated graphs grows.

paragraphs: The Randomized Dependence Coefficient, or RDC, measures nonlinear dependence between random variables that may have arbitrary dimension. Its starting point is the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi maximum correlation coefficient. The paper turns that motivation into a measure built from random nonlinear projections and correlations between the resulting representations.

These projections use copula representations, connecting the construction to dependence apart from the individual marginal distributions. The stated invariance to marginal distribution transformations means the measure is designed to preserve its assessment when those marginal descriptions change. This property matters when the relationship between variables is the object of interest, rather than the particular distributions each variable follows on its own.

The authors emphasize practicality alongside the statistical construction. RDC has low computational cost and can be implemented in five lines of R code, which the paper supplies. The contribution therefore combines a nonlinear, multidimensional dependence measure with a compact implementation. Its appeal lies in making a maximum-correlation-inspired approach accessible for computation while retaining the stated invariance property.
neurips-2013-the-randomized-dependence-c.tldr: RDC measures nonlinear dependence through random copula projections, combining marginal-transformation invariance with low computational cost.

paragraphs: Thompson Sampling had been demonstrated in complex bandit settings, but the available parametric guarantees discussed in this paper were limited to Bernoulli rewards. The authors extend the theory to one-dimensional exponential-family bandits. Their central result proves asymptotic optimality when the algorithm uses the Jeffreys prior.

The proof uses the structure of exponential families, particularly closed-form expressions for Kullback-Leibler divergence and Fisher information. These quantities also support the construction of the Jeffreys prior. This links the distribution family and prior choice directly to the argument establishing the algorithm's long-run performance.

The analysis additionally yields a finite-time exponential concentration inequality for posterior distributions in exponential families. That result describes posterior concentration and may be useful beyond the bandit proof itself. The covered distributions include some heavy-tailed exponential families for which the authors report that no optimistic algorithm had yet been proposed. The contribution broadens the theoretical foundation of Thompson Sampling while keeping its optimality claim tied to the stated family, prior, and asymptotic setting.
neurips-2013-thompson-sampling-for-1-dim.tldr: Thompson Sampling with the Jeffreys prior is asymptotically optimal for one-dimensional exponential-family bandits.

paragraphs: Binary matrices can record sensitive facts such as group memberships or purchase histories. Row and column totals are often released because they appear less revealing than individual entries. This paper investigates how those totals can nevertheless support inferences about particular cells of the hidden matrix.

The method treats the supplied totals as constraints defining a space of compatible matrices. It does not assume a generative model for the original matrix. Instead, it computes probability distributions for entries of interest through implicit sampling of the compatible data space. The procedure handles all cells simultaneously without explicitly generating complete matrix realizations.

The resulting algorithm takes as much time as standard sampling methods need to generate just one compatible dataset. Experiments demonstrate its efficiency and effectiveness across multiple settings. The finding gives aggregate information a concrete interpretation: row and column totals restrict possible underlying datasets enough to support cell-level inference. The output is probabilistic information about entries, allowing the framework to characterize what those constraints reveal without claiming exact reconstruction of every hidden value.
neurips-2013-what-do-row-and-column-marg.tldr: An efficient algorithm uses row and column totals to infer probabilities for hidden binary-matrix entries without generating complete datasets.
